newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Key Thai indicators confirm lingering slump.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Key Thai indicators confirm lingering slump.

text.p: The Bank of Thailand on Thursday announced weak April and May economic indicators confirming market expectations the slumping Thai economy will take time to recover.

Analysts said a $4 billion decline in Thai foreign reserves in May to $33.3 billion was largely in line with market expectations after the central bank intervened aggressively in offshore markets to defend the baht during a mid-May attack.

But they were surprised by relatively high monthly imports of 151.4 billion baht ($6.06 billion) in April, against 149.1 billion in March, which widened the April trade deficit to a 12-month high of 41.0 billion baht.
The deficit stood at 22.2 billion baht in March and 51.1 billion in April 1996.

"April imports were very high given the fairly depressed state of the economy. The increase may have been due to a rise in capital goods and machinery imports and the impact of the reversal of the yen/dollar rate," said Sriyan Pietersz, chief strategist of Capital Nomura Securities Plc.
The central bank said April imports included the cost of a commercial satellite Thaicom 3 bought by Shinawatra Satellite Plc.
Thailand has been sliding into its worst economic crisis in over a decade with growth seen falling sharply to 5.6 percent this year from 6.4 percent registered in 1996.

The finance sector is in deep trouble, heavily exposed to the depressed property sector and hit by a liquidity crunch in a high interest rate environment. The stock market has slumped to eight year lows and the baht has come under attack.
Central bank chief economist Kleo-thong Hetrakul said May foreign reserves fell to a two-year low of $33.3 billion from $37.3 billion in April.
She said apart from the central bank intervention on behalf of the baht, Thai corporate borrowers also rushed to repay offshore loans last month when the dollar eased against other currencies.

The drain on foreign reserve was reflected in the May balance of payments which posted a 112.3 billion baht deficit, rocketing from 15.5 billion in April and against a 7.7 billion baht surplus a year ago.

Vuth Puthamon of Multi-Credit Corp of Thailand Plc said although the reduced reserves still could finance about 5.8 months of imports, he expected them to continue declining in the next few months as the central bank had taken both spot and forward positions to defend the baht last month.
The central bank said the April current account deficit also widened to a year high of 38.0 billion baht from 15.9 billion in March.
Vuth of MCC said manufacturing output, private investment, bank credits and M-2 money supply also sustained their downward trends in April and May.

Some analysts, however, were surprised that the stock market did not react to the central bank's negative figures. The composite SET Index closed Thursday up 4.84 percent, largely fuelled by foreign bargain hunting for deeply discounted bank and communications stocks.
"The market feels that stocks have come down far enough. People just don't like to miss the rebound," a foreign analyst said.
Bank and communications counters gained 6.58 and 6.42 percent on Thursday.
